The Blackfin flounder Glyptocephalus stelleri is a commercially valuable pleuronectid inhabiting the continental shelf of the northwestern Pacific. Based on the reported length-weight relationship, the maximum body mass attained by adult females is 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams], a figure derived from the largest individuals collected during trawl surveys in the Sea of Okhotsk. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs measuring approximately 0.5 millimeters in diameter, yielding an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.000066 grams [Wwb = 0.000066 grams]. This extraordinarily small hatchling mass is typical of flatfishes that produce highly yolked eggs, though it nevertheless imposes a severe constraint on early larval survivorship. Field studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 4.8 °C [T = 4.8 °C] have shown that the yolk-sac larva completes its endotrophic phase remarkably quickly, with eclosion from the chorion occurring after 8 days [ab = 8 days] under those cold conditions. The brevity of this egg stage likely reflects an adaptation to the cold, food-poor waters of the subarctic Pacific, where rapid transition to the exogenously feeding larval stage is critical.

As the individual progresses through the pelagic larval phase, a pronounced allometric reorganisation of the body plan accompanies the benthic settlement transition. Growth trajectories compiled from otolith-incremented age assignments indicate that female Blackfin flounder attain a total length of 26.3 centimeters [Lp = 26.3 centimeters] at the onset of sexual maturation, a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 134.6 grams [Wwp = 134.6 grams] according to the standard length-weight conversion. These pubertal dimensions are modest relative to the species' ultimate size, suggesting that reproduction begins well before somatic growth is complete. The length at which 50% of females become reproductively active, derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue, is generally consistent with the 26.3 centimeter benchmark, although some regional variation has been noted in populations from the southern Kuril Islands compared to those from the northern Sea of Japan.

The maximum recorded total length for Glyptocephalus stelleri is 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters], a value obtained from a large female captured during a research cruise in the eastern Tatar Strait. In contrast to the length at puberty, this ultimate total length represents an asymptotic size approached only after many years of growth in the cold, resource-limited waters of its native range. Annual growth increments decline sharply once individuals exceed approximately 40 centimeters, with the remaining somatic expansion proceeding at a rate of only 1 to 2 centimeters per year. The asymptotic mass corresponding to this length, as predicted by the length-weight relationship, approaches the 1500 gram [Wwi = 1500 gram] maximum recorded in the literature, though our own data suggest that most females plateau at around 1144 grams under typical environmental conditions. This modest maximum size, compared to other large pleuronectids such as the Pacific halibut, constrains the species' fecundity and overall reproductive output.

Reproductive investment in the Blackfin flounder is closely tied to the cold thermal regime of its deepwater habitat. Under the sustained temperature of 4.8 °C [T = 4.8 °C] that characterises the spawning grounds, each mature female produces an average of 278 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 278 eggs per spawning event] based on annual fecundity estimates from ovarian biopsies. Field observations indicate that individual females spawn approximately once per year [F_R_i = spawn approximately once per year], yielding a daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.762 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.762 eggs per day]. This annual spawning periodicity is low compared to temperate flatfishes but consistent with the slow metabolic pace of subarctic marine teleosts. The combination of a modest batch size and annual frequency results in a relatively low lifetime fecundity that is offset by the high lipid content and large diameter of the individual eggs, shifting the reproductive allocation toward per-offspring investment rather than total numerical output.

Longevity estimates for Glyptocephalus stelleri are based on otolith readings from the oldest individuals sampled in commercial bycatch and scientific surveys. The maximum lifespan recorded under natural conditions is 23 years [am = 23 years] when measured at the typical thermal regime of 4.8 °C [T = 4.8 °C] that prevails over much of its depth range. This protracted lifespan is notable among western Pacific pleuronectids and is comparable to that of the Greenland halibut, another cold-adapted flatfish sharing similar physiological constraints. The combination of delayed puberty at 26.3 centimeters total length and a long adult phase underscores an iterative, low-risk life-history strategy in which adult mortality is kept low and reproductive effort is distributed across many seasons. Senescent individuals show a gradual decline in feeding activity and gonadal function, but direct causes of natural mortality remain poorly documented, with predation by Pacific cod and Steller sea lions being the most frequently cited sources.
